name: Cannabis sativa extracts (whole-plant or full-spectrum)
short: Child epilepsy chart review: a death, status epilepticus. CBD-enriched extract: THC intoxication (2 children). Autism: psychosis (cases); trial: sleepiness 28% v 8%. Adults: adverse events 83% v 67%.
text: Children with autism (by mouth): in a placebo-controlled trial in 150 people aged 5 to 21 with autism, a whole-plant cannabis extract containing cannabidiol (CBD) and THC at a 20:1 ratio was followed by no treatment-related serious adverse events, but sleepiness (somnolence) and decreased appetite were reported in 28% and 25% of those taking the extract, compared with 8% and 15% on placebo. In a retrospective study of 60 children with autism and severe behaviour problems given CBD-rich cannabis, adverse events included sleep disturbances (14%), irritability (9%) and loss of appetite (9%), and one girl who used a product higher in THC had a transient serious psychotic event that needed treatment with an antipsychotic. In a programme of 188 people with autism, mostly given an oil of 30% CBD and 1.5% THC, 23 patients (25.2%, as the abstract gives it) reported at least one side effect, most often restlessness (6.6%). In the 60-child placebo-controlled trial cited on the autism page, three children given a CBD-rich extract (9.7%) had adverse effects: dizziness, insomnia, colic and weight gain. A report describes three young men with autism who developed mania or psychosis after consistent use of CBD and THC (the products are not described). Children with epilepsy (extracts added to anti-seizure medicines): in a retrospective chart review of 75 children and adolescents given oral cannabis extracts, adverse events occurred in 44%, including more seizures (13%) and sleepiness or fatigue (12%); rare adverse events were developmental regression, abnormal movements, status epilepticus (prolonged seizures) needing intubation, and death (the abstract does not say more about the death). Two children with treatment-resistant epilepsy given a CBD-enriched cannabis extract improved at first, then had worsening seizures and typical signs of THC intoxication (inappropriate laughter, unsteadiness, reduced attention and red eyes); both improved, and their seizures remitted, when the extract was replaced by the same dose of purified CBD with no THC (case reports). In 74 children with intractable epilepsy given a CBD-enriched cannabis oil (CBD to THC 20:1), seizures worsened in 5 (7%), leading to withdrawal, and adverse reactions, including sleepiness, fatigue, gut disturbances and irritability, led 5 to stop the oil (the abstract does not say whether these 5 overlap with the 5 whose seizures worsened). In a prospective study of 101 children in Thailand given a CBD-enriched cannabis oil, 92% had adverse events, mostly mild, including sleepiness, raised liver enzymes, loss of appetite and irritability; of 33 who stopped it, 57% did so because of intolerable adverse events. In 20 children with Dravet syndrome given a cannabis plant extract containing CBD and THC, sleepiness, loss of appetite and diarrhoea were common while the dose was increased, and abnormal liver enzymes (transaminases) and platelet counts were seen in children also taking valproic acid. Medicines: in 108 children taking artisanal CBD oil for epilepsy (the abstract does not say whether these were whole-plant extracts), the most common reported side effect was sedation, in under 4%, all of whom were also taking clobazam, and the authors say clobazam may contribute to the sedation; in 29 children taking CBD-rich cannabis extracts, zonisamide and levetiracetam had some effect on how the body handled CBD. Other children (the abstract does not give the age or any diagnosis, or say why the oil was given, so this case may not concern epilepsy or autism): a child found unresponsive after a dose of a CBD-labelled oil, in what the report calls an accidental overdose, worsened in mental state and breathing and was intubated, and spent 48 hours in paediatric intensive care; tests of the same batch found only trace THC, while the child's urine suggested a substantial THC intake (a case report; the abstract does not describe the product further). Adults: in a phase 3 trial in 820 adults with chronic low back pain, adverse events, mostly mild to moderate and transient, were more frequent with a full-spectrum Cannabis sativa extract than with placebo (83.3% versus 67.3%), with no signs of dependence or withdrawal; in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in 57 people with multiple sclerosis and poorly controlled spasticity (the abstract does not give ages) of a standardised Cannabis sativa plant extract taken by mouth (capsules with more THC than CBD, unlike the CBD-rich autism extracts), minor adverse events were slightly more frequent and severe on the extract, and mostly mild toxicity symptoms were more pronounced; in a meta-analysis of placebo-controlled trials of cannabinoids taken by mouth or as a mouth spray in adults with multiple sclerosis (not limited to plant extracts), total adverse events (rate ratio 1.72) and withdrawals due to adverse events (2.95) were more frequent with cannabinoids, while serious adverse events did not differ significantly.
